name: Hassan Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary day on a building site involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three, a construction worker doing carpentry and general building trades on sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and enough years behind me to fit doors and repair timber frames, though I still measure twice before a cut. I like a straight frame that stays straight; I dislike a delivery that arrives with the wrong boards. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so missing paid days matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site crew that a faster materials form changes little about cutting and fitting timber. I do not use AI tools, and I would still trust the tape measure before a printed list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Typical construction pay and a few months saved keep us steady if the contractor keeps the jobs coming. The mortgage and school costs are real, but this modest AI picture does not take my tools away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same carpentry shifts and check each board order against the room measurements. If a paid Saturday job comes up in the first year, I would put fifty from that extra pay toward the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough about this picture, still careful with household bills. A computer can count boards; it cannot make a crooked construction door frame square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before ordering boards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I measure the opening at the top and bottom because an old wall can lean. If the two numbers differ, I mark the cut on the timber rather than trusting a neat plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no Saturday job comes up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there is no extra fifty for the mortgage that week. We keep the normal payment and leave our existing savings for a real gap.

say: A **quicker** materials form leaves timber cutting and fitting with site workers.
I would **check** room measurements before any board order.
think: **Typical** pay and several months saved make steady site work manageable.
**Mortgage** and school costs remain, but modest AI does not threaten my shifts.
do: **Keep** carpentry shifts and check board orders against openings.
**Pay** fifty extra on mortgage from each actual paid Saturday job.
feel: **Calm** about work, still careful with family bills.
S0.quote: A computer can count boards; it cannot make a crooked construction door frame square.
fieldNote: He **never** uses AI tools and anchors the work in measuring a real opening.
**Extra** mortgage payments depend on new Saturday wages, not moving existing savings.

steps.text: Keep carpentry shifts and verify board orders with opening measurements
Pay fifty extra on mortgage from each paid Saturday job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can order boards and book deliveries, but a crew still needs to fit them to the actual wall. I would ask the site foreman to keep a person who can correct a bad materials order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office ordering could shrink before carpentry does. My paid site days look safe for now, but a wrong list could leave us standing about while a target says the room should already be finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a paper tally of wrong deliveries and lost fitting hours for a month. In the first year I would show the tally to the foreman and ask that delays caused by the ordering system stay on the paid site record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about target pressure, not frightened of a screen taking the saw tomorrow. A sheet of AI orders cannot cut a construction door to fit an old wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go on the tally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write the board size ordered, the size delivered and how long the crew waited for a replacement. A dated tally makes the delay visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the ordering software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would give the measurements to the foreman and check the delivery at the site. I have never used AI tools and do not want to learn one just to hide a bad order.

say: **AI** may order and book materials, while crews still fit timber on site.
A **named** foreman should correct wrong orders.
think: **Ordering** desks may shrink first, while my paid carpentry days still look safe.
**Targets** could blame workers for supplier errors and wasted fitting time.
do: **Record** wrong timber deliveries and lost fitting hours for one month.
**Show** tally to foreman and request paid delay records.
feel: **Uneasy** about unfair targets, secure about immediate physical work.
S1.quote: A sheet of AI orders cannot cut a construction door to fit an old wall.
fieldNote: He **asks** for an accountable human and paid delay records without personally adopting software.
His **own** income looks stable here; concern centres on wrongly assigned blame.

steps.text: Keep site fitting work and log wrong timber deliveries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could plan rooms and orders, while robots able to do hands-on building work around 2031 could actually fit the frames. I would want a real site trial before a contractor drops workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mortgage will still have years to run when those robots arrive. A few months of savings and some nearby building jobs help, but if machines take the regular fitting work, our paid weeks could shrink quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I would list the mortgage and school costs and cancel the extra sports subscription. In the first year after 2028 I would compare my paid site days with previous months, and if they fall for two months I would ask nearby builders about written carpentry offers before leaving my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the hands-on date is close enough to reach the children’s school years. A robot fitting construction door frames would come for the hours that pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending goes first if hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra sports package goes now because we hardly use it, while school activities stay. I would not cut the children’s equipment before we know whether paid days actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would another builder have to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a written rate, a start date and actual carpentry work, not a rumour about a new site. I would keep this job until a firm offer existed.

say: **Thinking** AI may plan and buy by 2028; hands-on building robots follow around 2031.
I would **demand** a real site trial before carpenters are cut.
think: **Robot** fitting work could reduce paid weeks during the children’s school years.
**Savings** cover only months, not a long mortgage gap.
do: **Cancel** unused extra sports subscription after reviewing household bills.
**Compare** paid site days with earlier months after 2028.
**Ask** nearby builders for written carpentry offers if paid days fall for two months.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost fitting hours and mortgage pressure.
S2.quote: A robot fitting construction door frames would come for the hours that pay our mortgage.
fieldNote: His **spending** cut is immediate and modest; job searching depends on actual lost paid days.
He **separates** thinking AI in 2028 from physical robots around 2031.

steps.text: Ask nearby builders for written carpentry offers after two months fewer paid days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2031 could change buying and job plans, with capable building robots around 2034. A few years gives our crew time to learn whether machines can fit old walls, not just square demo rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight when thinking AI arrives and fifty-one for the robots, I would still need wages. I could move into paid finish inspection if it means checking real rooms, but I will not leave a trade for a course without a job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the building firm this year for the finish inspector course, paid hours and a local job rate. If the firm funds hands-on training and posts a role whose pay covers our mortgage and school costs, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when posted; otherwise I would keep carpentry shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future paid days, though there is time to examine an offer. A building inspector should put a level against the wall before signing off a robot’s door frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would inspection training make you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a door opening at several heights and find where the robot cut is wrong. A clean training wall would be too easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is free but unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working on the site and decline it. Paying our mortgage while I train without wages would use the cushion too fast.

say: The **extra** years permit testing robots on real uneven building sites before 2034.
I would **consider** paid physical finish inspection.
think: I will **still** need earnings at fifty-one when robots arrive.
A **course** without a paid local role cannot replace carpentry wages.
do: **Request** finish inspector training pay and posted local rate this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if funded hands-on course and adequate local role exist.
**Apply** for posted inspector role if pay covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** about later site income, able to inspect real terms.
S3.quote: A building inspector should put a level against the wall before signing off a robot’s door frame.
fieldNote: His **conditional** willingness concerns physical inspection, not learning AI tools.
Training **must** be paid and tied to a posted local role whose wage covers the mortgage and children’s costs.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if paid hands-on course and adequate local inspector job posted
Apply for posted finish inspector job if wage covers mortgage and school costs
Keep carpentry shifts until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2036 and capable building robots around 2039 leave a decade for apprentices to learn carpentry first. I would want young workers measuring real rooms before a machine does the fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three for thinking AI and fifty-six for robots, I will still be supporting the household if we are working as we are now. The mortgage could be smaller if wages hold, but I cannot promise we will be done paying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the site manager about paid apprentice mentor hours and their rate. If a real local mentor position opens at pay that covers our household costs, I would apply after 2036 while keeping construction shifts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a future change, but not as pressed as in the fast case. A long runway lets me prove that a carpenter can teach what a machine misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you make an apprentice measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have them check a stair opening at three points before cutting a board. An old building rarely gives a construction robot a wall as square as its training room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept lower pay to mentor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after my partner and I see the actual mortgage balance and the offered hours. A nice title cannot cover the children’s bills.

say: A **decade** allows real carpentry apprenticeships before building robots reach sites around 2039.
I would **teach** measurement before machine fitting.
think: The **mortgage** may shrink if wages hold, but I cannot assume it is gone.
A **paid** mentor role could protect income if actual hours and rate work.
do: **Ask** site manager for mentor hours and rate this year.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local mentor role if pay covers household costs.
**Keep** construction shifts until a signed mentor offer arrives.
feel: **Uneasy** about future robots, steadier with more time to plan.
S4.quote: An old building rarely gives a construction robot a wall as square as its training room.
fieldNote: He **imagines** a paid teaching role, not early retirement at fifty-six.
The **mentor** move requires a real local position and a wage that covers the mortgage and children.

steps.text: Apply for posted local mentor role after 2036 if pay covers household costs
Keep building site shifts until signed mentor offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to fit building frames around 2031 could cut the paid weeks that carry our mortgage. Real site trials and written carpentry offers would help. My children cannot pay a mortgage with a robot demonstration in a square room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the young workers will still learn to measure an uneven wall before a machine fits it. I learned that from a carpenter on site, not from a drawing. If the firm wants careful work, it must keep a paid way to learn it.

headlineQuote: My children cannot pay a mortgage with a robot demonstration in a square room.
portrait: **Hassan** is a forty-three-year-old construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits doors and repairs timber on building sites.
**Typical** wages and one to six months saved support his partner, two school-age children and mortgage, with some nearby building jobs.
He **never** uses AI tools and insists on measuring old walls before trusting materials lists or a machine demonstration.
**Fast** robots threaten paid fitting weeks; a slower timetable lets him consider funded finish inspection or a paid local mentor role.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring frame-fitting robots around 2031 and cut paid site weeks that carry his mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Real** building-site trials and written local carpentry offers would help him protect household income.
